goals: Locate the d-block in the periodic table, define a transition element and name important ores of 3d metals
Write electronic configurations of 3d elements and their ions, including chromium and copper, and note anomalies in the 4d and 5d series
Explain the trends in metallic character, atomic and ionic radii and ionisation enthalpy across the 3d series

slides.narration: Namaste! Iron in bridges, copper in wiring, titanium in aircraft, chromium on taps and gold in jewellery are all d-block metals, the elements in the middle of the periodic table. In this part we locate them, write their electronic configurations, and look at how their size and ionisation enthalpy change across the first series.

slides.heading: Position and definition
slides.body_md: The **d-block** occupies groups 3–12 in periods 4–7: the **3d** (Sc–Zn), **4d** (Y–Cd), **5d** (La, Hf–Hg) and **6d** (Ac, Rf–Cn) series. A **transition element** has an **incompletely filled d subshell** in its ground state or in one of its common oxidation states. Zn, Cd and Hg (d¹⁰ in atom and common ions) are d-block elements but not typical transition elements.

visual.alt: Table of the four d-series

slides.narration: The d-block sits between the s-block and the p-block, in groups three to twelve, with one series in each period from four to seven. A transition element has an incomplete d subshell, either in the atom or in a common ion. Copper qualifies because copper two plus is d nine; zinc does not, because both the atom and its ion have a full set of ten d electrons.

slides.heading: Occurrence of the 3d metals
slides.body_md: Most 3d metals occur combined in ores — oxides, sulfides and carbonates. Iron, titanium and manganese are abundant; copper and gold also occur native (free).

visual.alt: Table of ores of 3d metals with their formulae

slides.narration: Transition metals are usually found combined with oxygen or sulfur. Iron comes from haematite and magnetite, titanium from ilmenite and rutile, chromium from chromite and manganese from pyrolusite, which we meet again when we make potassium permanganate. Copper comes mainly from copper pyrites, though, like gold, it is sometimes found as the free metal.

slides.heading: Electronic configurations of the 3d series
slides.body_md: General configuration $(n-1)d^{1\text{–}10}ns^{1\text{–}2}$. **Chromium** and **copper** are exceptions: a half-filled ($d^5$) or completely filled ($d^{10}$) subshell has extra stability (exchange energy and symmetry), and 3d and 4s are close in energy.

visual.alt: Table of the electronic configurations of the 3d elements

slides.narration: Across the three d series, electrons enter the three d orbitals while the four s holds one or two. Chromium is three d five, four s one, and copper is three d ten, four s one, because a half-filled or completely filled d subshell is especially stable and the three d and four s levels are very close in energy. Learn these two exceptions well.

slides.heading: Configurations in the 4d and 5d series
slides.body_md: In the heavier series the (n−1)d and ns energies are even closer, so irregular configurations are more common and do not always follow the d⁵/d¹⁰ rule.

visual.alt: Table of some configurations in the 4d and 5d series

slides.narration: In the second and third series, the d and s levels are so close that several elements have unusual configurations. Molybdenum resembles chromium and silver resembles copper, but palladium has no five s electron at all, and tungsten, in the same group as chromium, keeps two six s electrons. You need not memorise every case, but you should recognise these as exceptions.

slides.heading: Worked example: configurations of ions
slides.body_md:
**Rule.** When a d-block atom forms a cation, the **ns electrons are removed first**.

**Problem.** Write the configurations of Co²⁺ (Co = 27), Cr³⁺ (Cr = 24), Ni²⁺ (Ni = 28) and Ti⁴⁺ (Ti = 22), and state which is a d⁰ ion.

**Step 1.** Co [Ar]3d⁷4s² → Co²⁺ [Ar]3d⁷. Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ → Cr³⁺ [Ar]3d³.

**Step 2.** Ni [Ar]3d⁸4s² → Ni²⁺ [Ar]3d⁸. Ti [Ar]3d²4s² → Ti⁴⁺ [Ar]3d⁰ — the d⁰ ion.

visual.alt: Table of ion configurations and unpaired electrons

slides.narration: The key rule: the four s electrons leave first, even though they were added first. Cobalt loses its two four s electrons to give cobalt two plus, three d seven. Chromium loses its single four s electron and two three d electrons to give three d three. Nickel two plus is three d eight, and titanium four plus has lost all four outer electrons, leaving no d electrons at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: configuration of an ion
slides.body_md: Choose the correct configuration of a 3d ion.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the atom first, then remove the four s electrons before any three d electrons.

slides.heading: Metallic character and physical properties
slides.body_md: All d-block elements are **metals**: lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors. Except Zn, Cd and Hg, they are hard with high melting and boiling points, because **unpaired d electrons join in metallic bonding**. Melting points and enthalpies of atomisation peak near the middle of each series.

rows: Rises to about V–Cr, then falls; Zn low
Number of unpaired d electrons in bonding

visual.alt: Table of physical property trends in the 3d series

slides.narration: Transition metals are typical metals but unusually hard and strong. Besides the outer s electrons, their unpaired d electrons also take part in metallic bonding, so bonding is strongest, and melting points highest, towards the middle of a series. Zinc, cadmium and mercury, with full d subshells, have weaker bonding; mercury is even a liquid at room temperature.

slides.heading: Atomic and ionic radii
slides.body_md: Across the 3d series radii fall at first and then stay **nearly constant**: each added electron enters the inner 3d subshell, whose poor shielding is balanced by repulsion between d electrons. Ionic radii of M²⁺ ions decrease gradually. Down a group, 4d radii exceed 3d, but **4d and 5d radii are almost equal** (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of the lanthanoid contraction.

visual.alt: Metallic radii of the 3d series from scandium to zinc: a sharp fall from 164 picometres at scandium to about 129 at chromium, then nearly constant around 125 to 137 in the middle and end of the series
visual.caption: Approximate values.

slides.narration: Across the series the nuclear charge rises by one each time, but the new electron goes into an inner d orbital. At first the radius shrinks quickly; after chromium the extra pull is balanced by repulsion among the d electrons, so the size hardly changes. Down a group the second-row elements are larger, but the third-row elements are almost exactly the same size as the second row, a result of the lanthanoid contraction that we meet in the next chapter.

slides.heading: Ionisation enthalpy
slides.body_md: First ionisation enthalpies rise only slowly and irregularly across the 3d series: the extra nuclear charge is nearly cancelled by shielding from 3d electrons. Zinc’s is high (stable 3d¹⁰4s²). Some second and third ionisation enthalpies are unusually high where a d⁵ or d¹⁰ configuration would be broken (Cr⁺, Cu⁺ → second; Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺ → third).

visual.alt: First ionisation enthalpies of the 3d elements rising slowly and irregularly from about 630 kilojoules per mole for scandium to about 760 for iron and cobalt, then jumping to about 906 for zinc
visual.caption: Approximate values; the high value for zinc reflects its stable 3d¹⁰4s² configuration.

slides.narration: Across the series the first ionisation enthalpy rises slowly and unevenly, because each new d electron shields the outer electrons and nearly cancels the extra nuclear charge. Zinc stands out with a high value from its filled sub-shells. The second ionisation enthalpies of chromium and copper are unusually high, because removing that electron destroys a half-filled or completely filled d subshell.

slides.heading: Worked example: explaining ionisation enthalpy anomalies
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain why (a) the second ionisation enthalpy of copper (1958 kJ mol⁻¹) is much higher than that of zinc (1733 kJ mol⁻¹), and (b) the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese is unusually high.

**(a)** Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰ (stable, filled); removing the second electron breaks this. Zn⁺ is 3d¹⁰4s¹; its second electron comes from 4s, leaving stable 3d¹⁰.

**(b)** Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ (stable, half-filled); removing a third electron destroys the half-filled subshell.

nodes.label: Does removal break d⁵ or d¹⁰?

visual.alt: Flow for explaining ionisation enthalpy anomalies

slides.narration: Ask which electron is being removed and what configuration is left. Removing the second electron from copper one plus breaks a completely filled d subshell, which costs a lot of energy. For zinc one plus the second electron comes from the four s, leaving a stable filled d subshell, so it is easier. In manganese two plus, removing a third electron breaks the half-filled d five subshell, so the third ionisation enthalpy is high.

decks.title: Transition (d-Block) Elements — Part 2: Oxidation states, colour, magnetism and other properties
goals: Explain why transition metals show variable oxidation states and identify common states in the 3d series
Relate the colour of transition metal ions to d–d transitions
Explain catalytic activity, complex formation, interstitial compounds and alloy formation

slides.heading: Characteristic properties
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the properties that make transition metals special.

visual.alt: Flow from partly filled d orbitals to the characteristic properties of transition metals

slides.narration: Why is copper sulfate blue, why can iron be iron two or iron three, why does a magnet attract some salts, and why are transition metals the best industrial catalysts? Almost every special property of these elements comes from their partly filled d orbitals. In this part we take each property in turn.

slides.heading: Variable oxidation states
slides.body_md: Because the (n−1)d and ns electrons have similar energies, transition elements show **several oxidation states**, often differing by one. In the 3d series the maximum rises to **+7 at Mn** (= number of 3d + 4s electrons), then falls. Higher states occur in oxides, fluorides and oxoanions (MnO₄⁻, Cr₂O₇²⁻); low states in complexes with π-acceptor ligands such as CO (Ni(CO)₄, oxidation state 0).

visual.alt: Table of common oxidation states of the 3d elements

slides.narration: Iron can be iron two or iron three; manganese ranges from plus two to plus seven. Because the three d and four s electrons are close in energy, different numbers of them can be used in bonding. Up to manganese, the highest state equals the total of three d and four s electrons; after that, pairing makes d electrons harder to use, and the maximum falls again.

slides.heading: Worked example: stability of oxidation states
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain (a) why Fe³⁺ is more stable than Fe²⁺, (b) why Mn²⁺ is more stable than Mn³⁺, and (c) why Sc shows only +3.

**(a)** Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ (half-filled, extra stable); Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) is easily oxidised to it.

**(b)** Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵; Mn³⁺ (3d⁴) readily gains an electron to reach d⁵, so it is a strong oxidising agent ($E^\circ_{\ce{Mn^3+/Mn^2+}} = +1.57\ \text{V}$).

**(c)** Sc [Ar]3d¹4s² loses all three outer electrons to reach the noble-gas configuration of Sc³⁺.

visual.alt: Table of ions and the configurations that explain their stability

slides.narration: Use the stability of half-filled and empty subshells. Iron three plus has five d electrons, a half-filled set, so iron two plus tends to be oxidised to it. Manganese two plus already has five d electrons, so manganese three plus grabs an electron to reach that state and is a strong oxidising agent. Scandium loses all three outer electrons to reach the configuration of argon, so plus three is its only state.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidation states
slides.body_md: Identify the highest oxidation state or the most stable state of a 3d element.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count three d plus four s electrons up to manganese, and look for empty, half-filled or completely filled d subshells.

slides.heading: Magnetic properties
slides.body_md: Substances with **unpaired electrons** are **paramagnetic**; with all electrons paired, **diamagnetic**. A few (Fe, Co, Ni) are **ferromagnetic**. The **spin-only magnetic moment**, in Bohr magnetons (BM): $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

visual.alt: Table of spin-only magnetic moments for zero to five unpaired electrons

slides.narration: Each unpaired electron acts like a tiny magnet, so ions with unpaired electrons are attracted into a magnetic field: they are paramagnetic. The spin-only formula gives the magnetic moment as the square root of n times n plus two Bohr magnetons. Turning it around, a measured moment tells us how many unpaired electrons an ion has.

slides.heading: Worked example: magnetic moments
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Calculate the spin-only magnetic moments of V³⁺ (V = 23) and Co²⁺ (Co = 27). Which is more paramagnetic?

**Step 1.** V³⁺: 3d², $n = 2$, $\mu = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83\ \text{BM}$.

**Step 2.** Co²⁺: 3d⁷ — five singly occupied orbitals, two of them then paired — $n = 3$, $\mu = \sqrt{3 \times 5} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\ \text{BM}$. Co²⁺ is more paramagnetic.

visual.alt: Table of the magnetic moment calculation

slides.narration: First find the number of d electrons in the ion, then fill the five d orbitals singly before pairing. Vanadium three plus has two d electrons, both unpaired, giving the square root of eight, about two point eight three. Cobalt two plus has seven: five go in singly and two pair up, leaving three unpaired, about three point eight seven. More unpaired electrons means stronger paramagnetism.

slides.heading: Coloured ions
slides.body_md: In a hydrated or complex ion, the five d orbitals split into sets of slightly different energy. A d electron can absorb visible light of a particular wavelength and jump to a higher set (**d–d transition**); the ion shows the **complementary colour**. **d⁰** and **d¹⁰** ions are colourless.

visual.alt: Table of colours of hydrated 3d ions

slides.narration: Why is copper sulfate solution blue? In the hydrated copper ion the d orbitals are split slightly in energy, and a d electron absorbs orange-red light to jump to the higher set. We see the light that remains, which is blue. Ions with no d electrons, like titanium four plus, or a full set, like zinc two plus, have no such jump available, so they are colourless.

slides.heading: Worked example: colourless or coloured?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Predict which of these are coloured in aqueous solution, giving reasons: Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, Ni²⁺, Sc³⁺, Fe³⁺. Why is anhydrous CuSO₄ white but CuSO₄·5H₂O blue?

**Step 1.** Ti⁴⁺ (d⁰), Sc³⁺ (d⁰) and Cu⁺ (d¹⁰): colourless — no d–d transition. Ni²⁺ (d⁸) and Fe³⁺ (d⁵): coloured.

**Step 2.** In anhydrous CuSO₄ there are no water ligands to split the d orbitals suitably, so no visible light is absorbed; in the hydrate, water ligands split the d orbitals and a d–d transition absorbs red light.

visual.alt: Table predicting colour from d configuration

slides.narration: Look at the d count. With no d electrons, or a completely full set, there can be no d to d jump, so the ion is colourless: titanium four plus, scandium three plus and copper one plus. Nickel two plus and iron three plus have partly filled d subshells and are coloured. Anhydrous copper sulfate is white because without water ligands the splitting does not allow absorption of visible light.

slides.heading: Quick check: colour and magnetism
slides.body_md: Pick the ion that is coloured and paramagnetic, or colourless and diamagnetic.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ions with no d electrons, or with a full set of ten, have no unpaired electrons and no d to d transitions.

slides.heading: Catalytic properties
slides.body_md: Transition metals and their compounds are excellent **catalysts** because they (i) show **variable oxidation states**, forming unstable intermediates, and (ii) provide a **large surface** on which reactants are **adsorbed**, weakening their bonds and lowering the activation energy.

rows: Oxidation of I⁻ by S₂O₈²⁻ (via Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺)

visual.alt: Table of transition-metal catalysts and the processes they catalyse

slides.narration: Transition metals are the world’s favourite catalysts. Iron speeds up ammonia manufacture, vanadium pentoxide sulfuric acid manufacture, and nickel the hardening of oils into vanaspati. They work in two ways: by switching between oxidation states, as iron three and iron two do in the reaction of iodide with peroxodisulfate, and by adsorbing reactants on their surfaces, weakening bonds and lowering the activation energy.

slides.heading: Complex formation
slides.body_md: Transition metal ions form a large number of **complexes**, because they are **small**, carry a **high charge** and have **vacant d orbitals** of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands.

visual.alt: Table of complexes of transition metals

slides.narration: Add ammonia to blue copper sulfate solution and it turns deep blue as tetraamminecopper two plus forms. Transition metal ions form such complexes readily because they are small and highly charged, so they attract lone pairs strongly, and they have empty d orbitals to accept those lone pairs. We study complexes in detail in chapters ten and eleven.

slides.heading: Interstitial compounds and alloys
slides.body_md: **Interstitial compounds** form when small atoms (H, B, C, N) occupy the holes in the metal lattice (TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆): they are hard, have high melting points, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert; they are often non-stoichiometric. **Alloys** form readily because transition metal atoms have **similar radii** and can replace one another in the lattice.

visual.alt: Table of transition-metal alloys and their uses

slides.narration: Small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen can slip into the gaps in a transition metal lattice, giving interstitial compounds such as titanium carbide, which are very hard and have very high melting points. And because transition metal atoms are similar in size, one can replace another in the lattice, so they form many useful alloys, such as stainless steel and brass.

slides.heading: Quick check: catalysis and alloys
slides.body_md: Explain why transition metals act as catalysts or form alloys and interstitial compounds.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of variable oxidation states, surface adsorption and similar atomic sizes.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Variable oxidation states from close (n−1)d and ns energies; maximum +7 at Mn.
Stability of d⁰, d⁵ and d¹⁰ explains many preferred states (Sc³⁺, Fe³⁺, Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺).
μ = √(n(n+2)) BM; paramagnetism from unpaired electrons.
Colour from d–d transitions; d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions colourless.
Catalysts (variable oxidation states, surface adsorption); complexes; interstitial compounds; alloys.

visual.alt: Summary table of properties and causes

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Transition metals show several oxidation states because their d and s electrons are close in energy, and the stability of empty, half-filled and filled d subshells explains which are preferred. Unpaired d electrons give paramagnetism and, with split d orbitals, colour. Their variable oxidation states and surfaces make them good catalysts, and their size lets them form complexes, interstitial compounds and alloys.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Count unpaired electrons by filling five d orbitals singly before pairing.
For colour, mention d–d transition, absorption of visible light and complementary colour.
Give both reasons for catalytic activity.
For interstitial compounds, give properties (hard, high-melting, inert).

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. Fill all five d orbitals singly before pairing when counting unpaired electrons, and remember the square root in the magnetic moment formula. For colour, mention d to d transitions and absorption of visible light. Give both reasons for catalytic activity. And describe interstitial compounds by their properties.

sections.heading: 1. Position, occurrence and electronic configuration
sections.body_md:
The d-block lies in **groups 3–12**, periods 4–7: 3d (Sc–Zn), 4d (Y–Cd), 5d (La, Hf–Hg), 6d (Ac, Rf–Cn). A **transition element** has an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in a common ion; Zn, Cd and Hg (d¹⁰ throughout) are not typical transition elements. Most 3d metals occur as oxide, sulfide or carbonate ores (haematite Fe₂O₃, chromite FeCr₂O₄, pyrolusite MnO₂, ilmenite FeTiO₃, copper pyrites CuFeS₂, zinc blende ZnS).

General configuration $(n-1)d^{1\text{–}10}ns^{1\text{–}2}$; **Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹** (extra stability of d⁵ and d¹⁰). Heavier series show more irregularities: Pd 4d¹⁰5s⁰, W 5d⁴6s², Pt 5d⁹6s¹. **Ions lose ns electrons first** (Fe²⁺ 3d⁶, Fe³⁺ 3d⁵).

key_terms.definition_md: An element whose atom or one of whose common ions has an incompletely filled d subshell.
The block of elements in which the last electron enters an (n−1)d subshell.

sections.heading: 2. Metallic character, radii and ionisation enthalpy
sections.body_md:
All are metals; most are hard, dense and high-melting because **unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding**; melting points and enthalpies of atomisation peak mid-series; Zn, Cd and Hg are soft and low-melting.

**Radii:** fall at the start of a series, then stay nearly constant (extra nuclear charge balanced by shielding and d–d repulsion). M²⁺ radii decrease gradually. 4d > 3d, but **4d ≈ 5d** (Zr 160, Hf 159 pm) — the **lanthanoid contraction**.

**Ionisation enthalpy:** rises slowly and irregularly. High where d⁵ or d¹⁰ is broken: ΔiH₂ of Cr and Cu, ΔiH₃ of Mn and Zn. ΔiH₁ of Zn is high (3d¹⁰4s²).

key_terms.definition_md: The steady decrease in size across the lanthanoids, which makes 5d elements almost the same size as the 4d elements above them.
The enthalpy needed to convert one mole of a metal into gaseous atoms; a measure of metallic bonding.

visual.alt: Metallic radii of the 3d series from scandium to zinc: a sharp fall from 164 picometres at scandium to about 129 at chromium, then nearly constant around 125 to 137 in the middle and end of the series

sections.heading: 3. Oxidation states and variable valency
sections.body_md:
(n−1)d and ns energies are close, so several oxidation states occur, often differing by one. Maximum rises to **+7 at Mn** (sum of 3d and 4s electrons) and then falls as d electrons pair. Highest states appear in oxides, fluorides and oxoanions (Mn₂O₇, VF₅, CrO₄²⁻); zero state in carbonyls (Ni(CO)₄). Lower oxides are basic (MnO), higher ones acidic (Mn₂O₇).

Stability: d⁰, d⁵ and d¹⁰ favoured — Sc³⁺ (d⁰) only; Fe³⁺ (d⁵) more stable than Fe²⁺; Mn²⁺ (d⁵) more stable than Mn³⁺, so Mn³⁺ is oxidising; Cr²⁺ is reducing (to d³ Cr³⁺). In water Cu²⁺ is more stable than Cu⁺ because of the large hydration enthalpy of Cu²⁺.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability of an element to show more than one oxidation state in its compounds.

sections.heading: 4. Colour and magnetic properties
sections.body_md:
**Colour:** ligands split the d orbitals; a d electron absorbs visible light and is promoted (**d–d transition**); the ion shows the **complementary colour**. d⁰ (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) and d¹⁰ (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) ions are colourless. Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; the hydrate is blue.

**Magnetism:** unpaired electrons → **paramagnetic**; all paired → **diamagnetic**; Fe, Co, Ni are **ferromagnetic**. Spin-only moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM. Fill five d orbitals singly before pairing.

key_terms.definition_md: Promotion of a d electron from a lower to a higher set of split d orbitals by absorption of visible light.
Attraction into a magnetic field, caused by unpaired electrons.
Weak repulsion by a magnetic field, shown when all electrons are paired.

sections.heading: 5. Catalysis, complexes, interstitial compounds and alloys
sections.body_md:
**Catalysts** because of (i) variable oxidation states (unstable intermediates, e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ in the iodide–peroxodisulfate reaction) and (ii) surfaces that adsorb reactants. Examples: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅ (contact), Ni (hydrogenation of oils), Pt/Rh (Ostwald).

**Complexes:** small, highly charged ions with vacant d orbitals of suitable energy accept lone pairs: [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.

**Interstitial compounds:** H, B, C or N in lattice holes (TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H); hard, high-melting, metallic conductors, inert, often non-stoichiometric.

**Alloys:** similar atomic radii allow substitution: stainless steel (Fe, Cr, Ni), brass (Cu, Zn), bronze (Cu, Sn), nichrome (Ni, Cr).

key_terms.definition_md: A compound formed when small atoms occupy holes in a metal lattice.
A homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when writing configurations of ions.
- Writing Cr as 3d⁴4s² or Cu as 3d⁹4s².
- Forgetting the square root in the spin-only formula, or pairing electrons before all five d orbitals are singly filled.
- Calling Zn²⁺ or Sc³⁺ coloured.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Reason questions (2 marks): the configuration involved and the stability argument (d⁰, d⁵ or d¹⁰).
- Magnetic moment (2–3 marks): configuration, number of unpaired electrons, substitution in √(n(n+2)).
- Catalysis (2 marks): both reasons with an example.

questions.stem_md: Mohr’s salt, used as a primary standard in titrations, contains the Fe²⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26). Its electronic configuration is:

[Ar]3d⁵4s¹
[Ar]3d⁵

questions.stem_md: Zinc, cadmium and mercury are placed in the d-block but are not regarded as typical transition elements. Explain, giving the configurations of the zinc atom and the Zn²⁺ ion.

answer.model_answer_md: They are in the d-block because their last electrons enter an (n−1)d subshell. Zn is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² and Zn²⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰; Cd and Hg are similar. Neither the atoms nor their common ions have an incompletely filled d subshell, so they lack typical transition properties (their compounds are white and diamagnetic, and they show essentially one oxidation state).

questions.solution_md: d-block position; d¹⁰ in atom and ion.

marking_scheme.step: d¹⁰ in atom and ion, so not transition

questions.stem_md: Silver (Z = 47) has the configuration [Kr]4d¹⁰5s¹, yet it is counted as a transition element. Explain, with reference to silver(II) fluoride, AgF₂.

answer.model_answer_md: A transition element needs an incomplete d subshell in the atom or in one of its ions. The silver atom has a full 4d¹⁰ set, but in AgF₂ silver is Ag²⁺, with configuration [Kr]4d⁹ — an incompletely filled d subshell. Hence silver is a transition element.

questions.solution_md: Ag²⁺ is 4d⁹.

questions.stem_md: Molybdenum (Z = 42) and tungsten (Z = 74) lie in the same group as chromium. Write their ground-state configurations and comment on the difference between them.

answer.model_answer_md: Mo: [Kr]4d⁵5s¹, which resembles Cr (3d⁵4s¹) — a half-filled d subshell. W: [Xe]4f¹⁴5d⁴6s², which does not follow the d⁵s¹ pattern. In the heavier series the (n−1)d and ns energies are so close that configurations do not follow a simple rule.

questions.solution_md: Mo 4d⁵5s¹; W 5d⁴6s².

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configurations of V³⁺ (V, Z = 23), Mn⁴⁺ (Mn, Z = 25) and Cu²⁺ (Cu, Z = 29), and state the number of unpaired electrons in each.

answer.model_answer_md: V [Ar]3d³4s² → V³⁺ [Ar]3d²: 2 unpaired. Mn [Ar]3d⁵4s² → Mn⁴⁺ [Ar]3d³: 3 unpaired. Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ → Cu²⁺ [Ar]3d⁹: 1 unpaired.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpy of zinc (906 kJ mol⁻¹) is much higher than that of copper (745 kJ mol⁻¹). The best explanation is:

options.text_md: zinc loses an electron from a completely filled 4s² subshell lying outside a full 3d¹⁰ set
zinc has a larger atomic radius than copper
zinc has fewer protons than copper
zinc’s outermost electron is in a 4p orbital

questions.solution_md: Zn is 3d¹⁰4s²: filled subshells are particularly stable, so ionisation needs more energy — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Among vanadium, chromium, copper and zinc, which metal has the lowest melting point, and why?

options.text_md: Vanadium, because it has the fewest d electrons
Chromium, because its d subshell is half-filled
Copper, because it is a good conductor of electricity
Zinc, because its filled 3d subshell takes no part in metallic bonding

questions.solution_md: Zn (3d¹⁰4s²) bonds only through its 4s electrons, so its metallic bonding is weak (m.p. about 420 °C) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The density of the 3d metals rises from about 3.0 g cm⁻³ for scandium to about 8.9 g cm⁻³ for copper. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: the number of 4s electrons increases steadily
the metals become more reactive along the series
the atomic radius increases sharply along the series
atomic mass increases while the atomic radius falls or stays nearly constant

questions.solution_md: More mass packed into a similar or smaller volume gives a higher density — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Of zinc, manganese, iron and copper, which has the highest second ionisation enthalpy?

options.text_md: Copper
Zinc
Manganese
Iron

questions.solution_md: Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰; the second electron must come from a filled d subshell (ΔiH₂ about 1958 kJ mol⁻¹) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the ions Mn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Co²⁺ and Ni²⁺ (high-spin, in aqueous solution) has the smallest radius?

options.text_md: Mn²⁺
Ni²⁺
Fe²⁺
Co²⁺

questions.solution_md: For ions of the same charge the radius decreases gradually as the nuclear charge increases: Ni²⁺ (about 69 pm) is smallest — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Zirconium (160 pm) and hafnium (159 pm) have almost the same atomic radius.

**Reason (R):** Hafnium atoms have one more electron shell than zirconium atoms.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but an extra shell would make hafnium larger; the similar size is due to the lanthanoid contraction, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mercury is a liquid at room temperature because its filled 5d¹⁰6s² electrons take very little part in metallic bonding.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With no unpaired d electrons, the metallic bonding in mercury is very weak.

questions.stem_md: The first and second ionisation enthalpies of copper are $745\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $1958\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert $0.50\ \text{mol}$ of gaseous copper atoms into gaseous Cu²⁺ ions.
questions.solution_md: Energy per mole $= 745 + 1958 = 2703\ \text{kJ}$; for 0.50 mol: $E = 0.50 \times 2703 = 1351.5\ \text{kJ}$.

questions.stem_md: The metallic radii of chromium, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper all lie between 125 and 129 pm. Explain why they are so similar.

answer.model_answer_md: Across the series each added electron enters the inner 3d subshell while the nuclear charge rises by one. The 3d electrons shield the outer 4s electrons and repel one another, so the increased attraction is almost cancelled. The effective pull on the outer electrons hardly changes, and the radius stays nearly constant.

questions.solution_md: Extra charge balanced by 3d shielding and repulsion.

questions.stem_md: Explain why transition metals such as vanadium and chromium are hard with high enthalpies of atomisation, and why these values are highest near the middle of each series.

answer.model_answer_md: Besides the ns electrons, unpaired (n−1)d electrons take part in metallic bonding, giving strong bonds, hardness and high enthalpies of atomisation. The number of unpaired d electrons is largest near the middle of the series (about d⁵), so bonding — and the enthalpy of atomisation — is greatest there; it falls as d electrons pair up.

questions.solution_md: Unpaired d electrons in bonding; maximum mid-series.

questions.stem_md: The first ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of Cr, Mn and Fe are 653, 717 and 762; their second ionisation enthalpies are 1592, 1509 and 1561. Explain (a) why the second ionisation enthalpy of Cr is higher than that of Mn, and (b) why the first values rise only slowly.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Cr⁺ is 3d⁵: removing a second electron breaks a stable half-filled subshell, which needs extra energy. Mn⁺ is 3d⁵4s¹: its second electron comes from 4s and leaves the stable 3d⁵ set, so ΔiH₂ is lower. (b) As the nuclear charge rises by one, the added electron goes into the inner 3d subshell and shields the 4s electrons, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer electron increases only slightly.

questions.solution_md: Cr⁺ d⁵ broken; Mn⁺ loses 4s; shielding.

questions.stem_md: The atomic radii of titanium, zirconium and hafnium are 147, 160 and 159 pm. Explain the change from titanium to zirconium and from zirconium to hafnium, and state one consequence for zirconium and hafnium.

answer.model_answer_md: Ti to Zr: zirconium has an extra electron shell, so it is larger. Zr to Hf: between them come the fourteen lanthanoids, whose 4f electrons shield poorly; the steady increase in effective nuclear charge (lanthanoid contraction) cancels the effect of the extra shell, so Hf is the same size as Zr. Consequence: Zr and Hf have very similar chemical properties and occur together, so they are very hard to separate.

questions.solution_md: Extra shell; lanthanoid contraction; hard to separate.

questions.stem_md: Scandium shows only the +3 oxidation state in its compounds, such as ScCl₃. The best reason is that:

options.text_md: Sc³⁺ has a half-filled 3d subshell
scandium has three unpaired 3d electrons
Sc³⁺ has the stable noble-gas configuration of argon
the 4s electrons of scandium cannot be removed

questions.solution_md: Sc [Ar]3d¹4s² loses all three outer electrons to reach [Ar] — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In nickel tetracarbonyl, Ni(CO)₄, formed in the Mond process for purifying nickel, the oxidation state of nickel is:
questions.solution_md: CO is a neutral ligand and the compound is neutral, so nickel is in the zero state — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Blue solutions of chromium(II) salts quickly turn green on standing in air. This shows that:

options.text_md: Cr²⁺ is an oxidising agent that is reduced to chromium metal
Cr³⁺ is less stable than Cr²⁺ in water
Cr²⁺ is a reducing agent that is oxidised to the more stable Cr³⁺ (3d³)
chromium shows only one oxidation state in water

questions.solution_md: Cr²⁺ (3d⁴) loses an electron to oxygen to form green Cr³⁺ (stable 3d³) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Why does the highest oxidation state of a 3d metal often appear in an oxide or fluoride, such as VF₅ or Mn₂O₇?

options.text_md: Oxygen and fluorine are good reducing agents
Oxides and fluorides are always ionic
Oxygen and fluorine are small and highly electronegative, so they stabilise high oxidation states
Oxygen and fluorine have vacant d orbitals

questions.solution_md: Small, very electronegative atoms (and multiple bonding by oxygen) stabilise high states — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In water, Cu⁺ disproportionates into Cu and Cu²⁺ although Cu⁺ has a stable 3d¹⁰ configuration. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: Cu²⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
Cu⁺ is a stronger reducing agent than copper metal
Cu²⁺ is smaller and so cannot be hydrated
the much larger hydration enthalpy of Cu²⁺ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy of copper

questions.solution_md: Small, doubly charged Cu²⁺ is strongly hydrated; this energy outweighs ΔiH₂ — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Manganese(III) acetate acts as a strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution.

**Reason (R):** Mn³⁺ readily gains an electron to reach the stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration of Mn²⁺.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the drive to reach d⁵ Mn²⁺ explains why Mn³⁺ oxidises — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Manganese(II) oxide, MnO, is basic, while manganese(VII) oxide, Mn₂O₇, is acidic.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Oxides in low oxidation states are basic; those in high oxidation states are acidic.

questions.stem_md: The highest oxidation state of manganese, found in the purple permanganate ion, is +___.
questions.solution_md: Manganese uses all five 3d and two 4s electrons: **+7**.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the oxidation state of vanadium in the orthovanadate ion, VO₄³⁻.
questions.solution_md: Let the oxidation state be $x$: $x + 4(-2) = -3$, so $x = -3 + 8 = 5$. Vanadium is in the +5 state.

questions.stem_md: Pale green iron(II) sulfate solution slowly turns yellow-brown when left open to the air. Explain using electronic configurations.

answer.model_answer_md: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. Fe³⁺, with a half-filled d subshell, is more stable, so atmospheric oxygen oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺; the yellow-brown colour is that of iron(III) species.

questions.solution_md: Fe²⁺ d⁶ oxidised to more stable d⁵ Fe³⁺.

questions.stem_md: Explain (a) why transition elements show variable oxidation states, (b) why the number of oxidation states in the 3d series rises up to manganese and then falls, and (c) why MnO is basic but Mn₂O₇ is acidic.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The (n−1)d and ns electrons have similar energies, so different numbers of them can be used in bonding. (b) Up to Mn the maximum state equals the total of 3d and 4s electrons (Mn +7); after Mn the d electrons are increasingly paired and held more strongly, so fewer are available and the maximum falls. (c) In MnO (+2) the metal behaves like a typical metal ion, giving a basic oxide; in Mn₂O₇ (+7) the highly charged centre forms covalent bonds with oxygen and the oxide reacts with water to give an acid (HMnO₄).

questions.solution_md: Close energies; pairing after Mn; low state basic, high state acidic.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Total electrons up to Mn; pairing after
(c) Low state basic, high state acidic

questions.stem_md: Using electronic configurations, explain: (a) Mn²⁺ salts are more stable than Mn³⁺ salts; (b) iron(III) chloride is more stable than iron(II) chloride in air; (c) titanium(IV) chloride is colourless. (Z: Ti 22, Mn 25, Fe 26)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ (half-filled, extra stable); Mn³⁺ is 3d⁴ and tends to gain an electron. (b) Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ (half-filled) while Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶, so Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺. (c) Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰: with no d electrons there is no d–d transition, so no visible light is absorbed.

questions.solution_md: d⁵ stability twice; d⁰ colourless.

questions.stem_md: Four aqueous solutions contain Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺, V³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ respectively. Which solution is coloured, and why?

options.text_md: The Zn²⁺ solution, because zinc has ten 3d electrons
The V³⁺ solution, because its two 3d electrons can undergo d–d transitions
The Sc³⁺ solution, because the ion has a high charge
The Ti⁴⁺ solution, because the ion is very small

questions.solution_md: Only V³⁺ (3d²) has a partly filled d subshell; Sc³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ are d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the ions Fe²⁺, V³⁺, Cu²⁺ and Mn²⁺ has a spin-only magnetic moment of 4.90 BM? (Z: V 23, Mn 25, Fe 26, Cu 29)

options.text_md: V³⁺
Fe²⁺
Cu²⁺
Mn²⁺

questions.solution_md: 4.90 BM = √24, so n = 4. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) has four unpaired electrons — option (b). V³⁺ has 2, Cu²⁺ 1, Mn²⁺ 5.

questions.stem_md: Aqueous Ti³⁺ ions absorb green-yellow light near 500 nm and appear purple. The colour arises because:

options.text_md: the ion emits purple light when heated
the 4s electron is removed by light
the single 3d electron is promoted to a higher set of d orbitals and the light not absorbed is seen
the ion reflects all wavelengths equally

questions.solution_md: A d–d transition absorbs part of the visible spectrum; we see the complementary colour — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A piece of cobalt is strongly attracted by a magnet and stays magnetised after the magnet is removed. This behaviour is called:

options.text_md: diamagnetism
ferromagnetism
weak paramagnetism
antiferromagnetism

questions.solution_md: Fe, Co and Ni show permanent magnetisation from aligned domains — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Aqueous solutions of scandium(III) sulfate are coloured.

**Reason (R):** The Sc³⁺ ion has no d electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: Sc³⁺ salts are colourless. R is true, and it explains why no d–d transition is possible — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Copper(I) iodide is white because the Cu⁺ ion has a completely filled 3d subshell.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transition can occur.

questions.stem_md: Spin-only magnetic moments of ions such as Cr³⁺ are expressed in Bohr ___.
questions.solution_md: Bohr **magnetons** (BM).

questions.stem_md: Match each hydrated 3d ion with the colour of its dilute aqueous solution.

options.text_md: Cu²⁺
Ni²⁺
Co²⁺
Ti³⁺

questions.solution_md: Cu²⁺ blue; Ni²⁺ green; Co²⁺ pink; Ti³⁺ purple.

questions.stem_md: Manganese(III) acetate is used as an oxidant in organic synthesis. Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of the Mn³⁺ ion (Mn, Z = 25), in BM.
questions.solution_md: Mn³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁴: four unpaired electrons, $n = 4$. $\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\ \text{BM}$.

questions.stem_md: Blue crystals of copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate are weakly attracted by a strong magnet. Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of the Cu²⁺ ion (Cu, Z = 29), in BM.
questions.solution_md: Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹: one unpaired electron, $n = 1$. $\mu = \sqrt{1 \times 3} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\ \text{BM}$.

questions.stem_md: A violet salt of vanadium has a measured magnetic moment of $3.87\ \text{BM}$. Using the spin-only formula, find the number of unpaired electrons in the vanadium ion.
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{n(n+2)} = 3.87$, so $n(n+2) \approx 15$, i.e. $n^2 + 2n - 15 = 0$. Then $n = \dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{4 + 60}}{2} = \dfrac{-2 + 8}{2} = 3$. Three unpaired electrons (V²⁺, 3d³).

questions.stem_md: A salt of cobalt has a measured magnetic moment of 3.87 BM. Find the number of unpaired electrons and decide whether the cobalt is present as Co²⁺ or as high-spin Co³⁺. (Co, Z = 27)

answer.model_answer_md: μ = √(n(n+2)) = 3.87 gives n(n+2) = 15, so n = 3. Co²⁺ is 3d⁷ (five orbitals singly filled, two paired): 3 unpaired. High-spin Co³⁺ is 3d⁶: 4 unpaired (4.90 BM). The salt contains Co²⁺.

questions.solution_md: n = 3; Co²⁺.

questions.stem_md: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is a white powder, but it turns blue when water is added to it. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: In the hydrate, water molecules act as ligands around Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) and split the d orbitals into sets of different energy. A d electron absorbs red-orange light and is promoted (d–d transition), so the complementary blue colour is seen. Without water ligands the splitting is not suitable for absorbing visible light, so the anhydrous salt is white.

questions.solution_md: Water ligands split d orbitals; d–d transition.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moments of Cr³⁺ (Z = 24), Fe²⁺ (Z = 26) and Cu⁺ (Z = 29). Which of these ions would be weakly repelled by a magnet?

answer.model_answer_md: Cr³⁺ 3d³, n = 3: μ = √15 ≈ 3.87 BM. Fe²⁺ 3d⁶, n = 4: μ = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM. Cu⁺ 3d¹⁰, n = 0: μ = 0. Cu⁺ is diamagnetic, so it is weakly repelled.

questions.solution_md: 3.87; 4.90; 0, Cu⁺ diamagnetic.

questions.stem_md: A solution of hydrated Ni²⁺ ions looks green. (a) What happens to the d electrons of Ni²⁺ when white light passes through the solution? (b) Why is the colour seen different from the colour absorbed? (c) Why does a solution of zinc sulfate show no colour?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Water ligands split the 3d orbitals of Ni²⁺ (3d⁸); an electron absorbs light of a particular visible wavelength and is promoted to the higher set (d–d transition). (b) The light that is not absorbed passes through; we see this transmitted, complementary colour (green), not the absorbed colour (red/violet). (c) Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: the d orbitals are full, so no d–d transition is possible and no visible light is absorbed.

questions.solution_md: d–d transition; complementary colour; Zn²⁺ d¹⁰.

questions.stem_md: A few drops of iron(III) solution greatly speed up the reaction between iodide and peroxodisulfate ions. The iron ions act mainly by:

options.text_md: adsorbing iodine molecules on their surface
raising the temperature of the mixture
forming an alloy with iodine
switching between the +3 and +2 states, carrying electrons from iodide to peroxodisulfate

questions.solution_md: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ and is reduced to Fe²⁺, which peroxodisulfate re-oxidises — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃?

options.text_md: Iron, with molybdenum as promoter
Vanadium pentoxide
Finely divided nickel
Platinum–rhodium gauze

questions.solution_md: Iron (promoted by Mo) — option (a). V₂O₅ is for the contact process (b).

questions.stem_md: Titanium carbide, TiC, used to coat cutting tools, is an interstitial compound. Which property would you expect it to have?

options.text_md: A low melting point and softness
High solubility in water as an ionic salt
A very high melting point and great hardness
No electrical conductivity at all

questions.solution_md: Small carbon atoms in the lattice holes make the solid harder and higher-melting, while it keeps metallic conductivity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Stainless steel, used for surgical instruments, resists rusting. Besides iron, its main alloying metals are:

options.text_md: copper and zinc
copper and tin
chromium and nickel
lead and tin

questions.solution_md: Stainless steel contains Cr (and Ni) — option (c); Cu/Zn is brass (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Transition metals readily form alloys such as brass and nichrome with one another.

**Reason (R):** All transition metals have the same number of d electrons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — the d electron count varies. Alloys form because the atomic radii are similar — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Interstitial compounds such as Mn₄N are softer and lower-melting than the pure metal.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. They are harder and have higher melting points than the parent metal.

questions.stem_md: A brass tap has a mass of $250\ \text{g}$ and contains 35% zinc by mass; the rest is copper. Calculate the mass of copper in the tap, in grams.

Nickel is used to hydrogenate vegetable oil into vanaspati, while vanadium pentoxide catalyses the oxidation of sulfur dioxide in the contact process. State the property of each catalyst that explains its action.

answer.model_answer_md: Nickel: its finely divided surface adsorbs hydrogen and the oil molecules, weakening their bonds and bringing them together, which lowers the activation energy. V₂O₅: vanadium changes oxidation state — V₂O₅ oxidises SO₂ and is reduced to V₂O₄, which air re-oxidises — so it works through variable oxidation states.

questions.solution_md: Ni: surface adsorption; V₂O₅: variable oxidation states.

questions.stem_md: What are interstitial compounds of transition metals? Give two examples and three of their characteristic properties.

answer.model_answer_md: They form when small atoms such as H, B, C or N occupy the holes (interstices) in the crystal lattice of a transition metal. Examples: TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆. Properties (any three): high melting points, higher than the pure metal; very hard; retain metallic conductivity; chemically inert; often non-stoichiometric.

questions.solution_md: Definition; TiC, Mn₄N; hard, high-melting, conducting.

questions.stem_md: Explain why transition metals readily form alloys. Name one alloy of copper and one alloy of nickel, giving the composition and one use of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Transition metal atoms have similar atomic radii and similar metallic bonding, so atoms of one metal can take the place of another in the crystal lattice. Copper: brass (Cu and Zn), used for taps and fittings — or bronze (Cu and Sn), for statues and medals. Nickel: nichrome (Ni and Cr), used for heating elements — or stainless steel (Fe, Cr, Ni), for cutlery.

questions.solution_md: Similar radii; brass; nichrome.

marking_scheme.step: Copper alloy with composition and use
Nickel alloy with composition and use

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define a transition element. Is copper a transition element? Give a reason. [1]

(b) Write the ground-state configurations of chromium (Z = 24) and molybdenum (Z = 42), and explain why each has only one outer s electron. [2]

(c) Explain the variation of atomic radius across the 3d series, and why the 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost the same radius. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An element with an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in a common ion. Copper is one: the atom is 3d¹⁰4s¹ but Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹.

(b) Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Mo: [Kr]4d⁵5s¹. The (n−1)d and ns levels are very close in energy, and a half-filled d⁵ subshell has extra stability (exchange energy), so one s electron moves into the d subshell.

(c) The radius falls at first as the nuclear charge increases, then stays almost constant because each added 3d electron shields the outer electrons and repels the other d electrons, balancing the extra nuclear charge. In a group, the 5d elements come after the lanthanoids; the poor shielding of 4f electrons causes the lanthanoid contraction, which cancels the expected increase in size, so 4d and 5d radii are almost equal (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm).

questions.solution_md: Definition; Cr and Mo d⁵s¹; radii trend and lanthanoid contraction.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why the first ionisation enthalpies of the 3d elements increase only slightly from scandium to copper. [1]

(b) The third ionisation enthalpy of manganese (3248 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of iron (2957 kJ mol⁻¹). Explain. [2]

(c) Melting points (°C): Ti 1668, V 1910, Cr 1907, Mn 1246, Fe 1538, Zn 420. Explain the high values for V and Cr and the low value for Zn. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Each additional electron enters the inner 3d subshell and shields the outer 4s electrons, almost cancelling the increase in nuclear charge, so the effective nuclear charge on the 4s electron rises only slightly.

(b) Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ (half-filled, extra stable); removing a third electron breaks this arrangement and needs more energy. Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶; removing one electron gives the stable 3d⁵ Fe³⁺, so less energy is needed.

(c) V (3d³4s²) and Cr (3d⁵4s¹) have many unpaired d electrons that take part in metallic bonding, so bonding is strong and melting points are high. Zn (3d¹⁰4s²) has no unpaired d electrons; only the 4s electrons bond, so its metallic bonding is weak and the melting point is low. (Mn is lower than expected because of its stable d⁵ arrangement and complex structure.)

questions.solution_md: Shielding; Mn²⁺ d⁵ vs Fe²⁺ d⁶; unpaired d electrons in bonding.

questions.stem_md:
(a) List the oxidation states shown by manganese and explain why +7 is the maximum. [1½]

(b) Cu⁺ has a stable 3d¹⁰ configuration, yet Cu²⁺ is the more stable ion in aqueous solution. Explain. [2]

(c) Of Ti²⁺, Ti³⁺ and Ti⁴⁺ (Ti, Z = 22), which is most stable, and which gives a colourless solution? Give reasons. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) +2, +3, +4, +5, +6 and +7. Mn is 3d⁵4s²: using all seven 3d and 4s electrons gives +7, so no higher state is possible.

(b) Although forming Cu²⁺ needs the large second ionisation enthalpy, Cu²⁺ is small and doubly charged, so its hydration enthalpy is much more negative than that of Cu⁺. This extra hydration energy outweighs the ionisation energy, so Cu²⁺(aq) is more stable and Cu⁺(aq) disproportionates: 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu.

(c) Ti⁴⁺ (3d⁰, the noble-gas configuration of argon) is the most stable. It is also colourless, because with no d electrons no d–d transition can occur.

questions.solution_md: +2 to +7; hydration enthalpy; Ti⁴⁺.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Ti⁴⁺ most stable and colourless, d⁰

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between paramagnetic and diamagnetic substances and write the spin-only formula for magnetic moment. [1]

(b) Calculate the spin-only magnetic moments of V²⁺ (V, Z = 23) and Cr²⁺ (Cr, Z = 24). [2]

(c) Explain why aqueous Ti³⁺ is purple but aqueous Ti⁴⁺ is colourless. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Paramagnetic substances have unpaired electrons and are attracted into a magnetic field; diamagnetic substances have all electrons paired and are weakly repelled. μ = √(n(n+2)) BM.

(b) V²⁺: 3d³, n = 3, μ = √15 ≈ 3.87 BM. Cr²⁺: 3d⁴, n = 4, μ = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.

(c) Ti³⁺ is 3d¹. Water ligands split the d orbitals; the single d electron absorbs green-yellow light and is promoted (d–d transition), so the complementary purple colour is seen. Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰ — no d electron to promote — so no visible light is absorbed and the solution is colourless.

questions.solution_md: Definitions and formula; 3.87 and 4.90 BM; d¹ vs d⁰.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Iron(III) ions catalyse the oxidation of iodide ions by peroxodisulfate ions. Write the two ionic equations for the catalysed path and name the property of transition metals it shows. Give one other reason why transition metals are good catalysts. [2]

(b) Why do transition metal ions form a large number of complexes? Give one example. [1½]

(c) What are interstitial compounds? State two of their properties. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{2Fe^3+ + 2I^- -> 2Fe^2+ + I2}$ and $\ce{S2O8^2- + 2Fe^2+ -> 2SO4^2- + 2Fe^3+}$. This shows variable oxidation states (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺). Another reason: transition metals provide a surface on which reactants are adsorbed, weakening their bonds (for example nickel in hydrogenation).

(b) The ions are small and highly charged, so they attract ligand lone pairs strongly, and they have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept the lone pairs. Example: the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) ion formed from Cu²⁺ and ammonia.

(c) Compounds formed when small atoms (H, B, C, N) occupy holes in the metal lattice, e.g. TiC. Properties (any two): very hard; high melting points; metallic conductivity; chemically inert.

questions.solution_md: Two equations; variable states and adsorption; small charged ions with vacant d orbitals; interstitial compounds.
